title: How to build a Figma-to-code design token pipeline — Part 1
partialText:
DESIGN SYSTEM GUIDE

How to build a Figma-to-code design token pipeline — Part 1

Learn how to connect Figma variables to your Angular project and keep your design system in sync using Style Dictionary.

In the previous articles, we covered how to integrate a CSS framework, structure your SCSS, build a color palette, and customize components beyond what variables alone allow. By the end of that series, your project had a centralized variables file and a clean customization layer on top of Bootstrap. This guide assumes you already have that setup in place. In this article, we take one step further — we connect the source of those variables directly to Figma.

What are design tokens

Design tokens are the single source of truth for the visual properties of your design system — colors, typography, spacing, and others. Instead of setting primary color in your styles and in design separately, you set it once in Figma and use it as a source of truth.

The problem tokens solve is drift. Over time, a color value in SCSS and the “same” color in Figma silently diverge. The designer updates the brand color in Figma. The developer doesn’t notice. Six months later, the product has two slightly different shades of blue in production. Sound familiar? If you’ve ever searched a hex value in your code trying to update it massively, you already know this problem firsthand.

Tokens fix such an issue by making the code the output of the design, not a copy of it — there’s no manual step to skip, because there’s only one place where the color can be defined.

In practice, the workflow looks like this:

  1. Figma (variables)
  2. tokens.json (export from Figma)
  3. Style Dictionary package in your project
  4. SCSS variables
  5. Bootstrap integrates color tokens in its palette

Figma variables setup

Let’s set up the Figma first. In your Figma file, open the Local variables panel, create a new collection named Brand and add six color variables:

Brand/primary   → #0d6efd
Brand/secondary → #6c757d
Brand/success   → #198754
Brand/info      → #0dcaf0
Brand/warning   → #ffc107
Brand/danger    → #dc3545

Such naming makes sense. The export feature in Figma uses the last segment of the variable path as the token key, case-sensitively — whatever case you type is what shows up in the JSON. So Brand/primary becomes the primary token, and so on — keep the last segment lowercase to match the token names Style Dictionary generates ($token-primary, not $token-Primary).

This means your Figma collection can be organized however you choose — Brand/colors/primary, Semantic/states/success — as long as the last segment matches. One rule to remember instead of a rigid folder structure to enforce? I'll take that trade every time.

Because those are native Figma Variables, anyone opening Dev Mode or the Inspect panel sees the variable name — Brand/primary — next to any layer that uses it.

Exporting variables to JSON

Here’s the part that’s easy to make overcomplicated: sync the token file with Figma.

If you use a plugin that pushes token changes straight into your GitHub repo, it sounds great, but it solves a problem this project doesn’t actually have. Brand colors don’t change often. A primary color can be modified once a year, but not weekly. Automating a rare event mostly adds a complexity that you don’t need. So it would be better to keep it simple.

Figma already has everything needed for that step. Open the Local variables panel, select the Brand collection, and click Export modes. Figma creates a .zip containing one file per mode, named after the mode — for a single-mode collection, unzip it and you get a file like tokens.json:

{
  "primary": {
    "$type": "color",
    "$value": {
      "colorSpace": "srgb",
      "components": [0.05098039, 0.43137255, 0.99215686],
      "alpha": 1,
      "hex": "#0d6efd"
    },
    "$extensions": {
      "com.figma.variableId": "VariableID:1:2",
      "com.figma.scopes": ["ALL_SCOPES"]
    }
  },
  // ...same shape for secondary, success, info, warning, danger
  "$extensions": { "com.figma.modeName": "Mode 1" }
}

This is a real token file — $type and $value are exactly what Style Dictionary expects — with one difference: $value is an object: colorSpace, components, alpha, hex, not a plain hex string. That shape difference is a config concern, not a hand-editing concern — the next section teaches Style Dictionary to read it as-is.

When you run the build locally and check the generated SCSS file, it allows you to properly test all the changes before deploying. In such a case there is no rushed auto-push to undo if a color turns out wrong.

Style Dictionary build

A pure declarative JSON config would be enough here if our tokens were already flat DTCG values — no custom code at all. Ours aren’t, quite: Figma’s export wraps each color in { colorSpace, components, alpha, hex } instead of a plain string, and no built-in transform understands that shape. That's the one thing our config needs to handle itself, through a small preprocessor — everything else can stay a built-in Style Dictionary transform, including the color output itself.

yarn add style-dictionary --dev

Create /src/sd.config.mjs:

import StyleDictionary from 'style-dictionary';

// Understands the raw file Figma's "Export modes" button produces —
// flattens {$value: {hex, ...}} to a plain hex string, drops the
// $extensions noise, and leaves the token names flat at the root.
StyleDictionary.registerPreprocessor({
    name: 'figma-export',
    preprocessor: (tokens) => {
        const { $extensions, ...rest } = tokens;
        return Object.fromEntries(
            Object.entries(rest).map(([name, t]) => [
                name,
                { $type: t.$type, $value: t.$value.hex ?? t.$value },
            ]),
        );
    },
});

export default {
    usesDtcg: true,
    preprocessors: ['figma-export'],
    source: ['design-tokens/tokens.json'],  // the file straight out of Figma's export zip
    platforms: {
        scss: {
            prefix: 'token',
            transforms: ['name/kebab', 'color/css'],  // primary → token-primary
            buildPath: 'src/styles/_/',
            files: [{
                destination: 'tokens.generated.scss',
                format: 'scss/variables',
                options: { outputReferences: true },
            }],
        },
    },
};

The figma-export preprocessor is the only custom piece, and it's the only reason this file is JS instead of JSON — everything below it (name/kebab, color/css, scss/variables) is a built-in Style Dictionary transform/format. Once the shape is flattened, this is a plain, declarative build — the same pattern you'd use for a Zeplin export or any other tool with its own token shape: point source at the file, teach Style Dictionary its structure, and let the rest of the pipeline stay generic.

Note: /design-tokens is added to .gitignore. Since the tokens.json file is used only to regenerate new SCSS variables, it doesn't make sense to keep it in the repo.

Point the build script at it via the Style Dictionary CLI in package.json:

{
  "scripts": {
    "tokens:build": "style-dictionary build --config src/sd.config.mjs"
  }
}

Run yarn tokens:build to generate the output file for the first time.

The generated output

After the build, you get src/styles/_/tokens.generated.scss:

// Do not edit directly, this file was auto-generated.
$token-primary: #0d6efd;
$token-secondary: #6c757d;
$token-success: #198754;
$token-info: #0dcaf0;
$token-warning: #ffc107;
$token-danger: #dc3545;

Notice that the file lives in the _/ subfolder — following the convention from the previous articles where such a folder holds all auto-generated SCSS files.

Note: if a later feature needs these values at runtime — a <canvas> context, a charting library, dynamic theming — that's the point to add CSS variables or TypeScript constants. Until then, the project only consumes colors at SCSS compile time.

Connecting tokens to Bootstrap

Let’s wire the tokens into Bootstrap’s theme now. The generated file lives in _/, so in src/styles/variables/_palette.scss we import it one level up and map the $token-* variables to Bootstrap's semantic color names:

// ── Design Tokens
// Source of truth: design-tokens/tokens.json
// To update: re-export from Figma (Local Variables → Export modes) → `yarn tokens:build`
@import '../_/tokens.generated';

// Map token variables → Bootstrap theme colors
$primary:   $token-primary;
$secondary: $token-secondary;
$success:   $token-success;
$info:      $token-info;
$warning:   $token-warning;
$danger:    $token-danger;

That’s the connection point. When Bootstrap generates its entire component system — buttons, badges, alerts, form validation states, focus rings — it uses $primary, $success, and the rest. By pointing those to $token-primary and friends, you've made the entire Bootstrap theme an output of your Figma file, not a translation of it.

The import order in vendor.scss is what makes this work:

// 1. Bootstrap functions (needed by everything else)
@import 'bootstrap/scss/functions';
// 2. Bootstrap defaults
@import 'bootstrap/scss/variables';

// 3. Our overrides — must come AFTER Bootstrap defaults
//    so we can use Bootstrap's own functions in our values
@import 'variables/variables';  // imports _palette.scss → ../_/tokens.generated.scss

// 4. Now Bootstrap can build its component system using our colors
@import 'bootstrap/scss/maps';
@import 'bootstrap/scss/mixins';
@import 'bootstrap/scss/utilities';
// ... component imports
The import order is critical. Our custom variables must come after Bootstrap’s defaults (step 3), because Bootstrap uses its own functions like tint-color() to generate shades. If we import our overrides before the functions are loaded, the build will fail.

The final result is a five-step variable chain:

  1. Figma variable — Brand/primary is set to #0d6efd.
  2. Export — clicking Export modes writes that value into tokens.json.
  3. Build — yarn tokens:build turns it into $token-primary: #0d6efd inside tokens.generated.scss (do not edit).
  4. Mapping — _palette.scss imports that file and sets $primary: $token-primary.
  5. Component output — Bootstrap’s variable system picks up $primary, so .btn-primary { background: $primary; }.

Change the color in Figma → export the mode again → run yarn tokens:build → every Bootstrap component updates automatically, on your own schedule.

Conclusion

In this article, we explored how to build a Figma-to-code design token pipeline around native Figma Variables and Figma’s own JSON export, with a review-gated build step instead of an unattended sync.

By the end, you should have:

  1. A Brand collection of native Figma Variables, exported to design-tokens/tokens.json file.
  2. A declarative Style Dictionary config with a small figma-export preprocessor, generating src/styles/_/tokens.generated.scssas SCSS variables.
  3. A new layer in _palette.scss that connects $token-* variables to Bootstrap's theme system.

In the next post, we’ll go deeper — connecting Figma to the pipeline with the Tokens Studio plugin and building an automated deploy process for teams where tokens change often enough that a manual export becomes the bottleneck. Stay tuned!

How to build a Figma-to-code design token pipeline — Part 1 was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Git Worktree, or: How I Stopped Losing My Afternoon to Hotfixes
partialText:
Drafted with AI assistance, based on my own workflow — reviewed and edited by me.

This happened to me today, so I’m writing it down while it’s fresh.

I’m in the middle of a database migration task on a feature branch for a SaaS project I’m building. The kind of work where your working directory is a mess by design — half-applied schema changes, a dev server running, three terminal tabs, and a very specific mental model of where everything is. Then someone flags a bug on main. Needs fixing today, not after my migration is done.

My first instinct was the usual routine. Stash everything, switch to main, fix, switch back, pop the stash, pray. I’ve done that dance a hundred times and I’ve been burned by it more than once — untracked files that didn’t stash, a pop that conflicted, twenty minutes rebuilding context that took hours to load in the first place.

Then I remembered git worktree exists. I’d read about it years ago and filed it under “neat, probably never need it.” Turns out today I needed it.

The one command

From my repo, still sitting on the migration branch, untouched:

git worktree add ../try-ai-receptionist-hotfix main

That creates a sibling folder with main checked out in it. Not a clone. Same repo, same history, same remotes — just a second working directory pointed at a different branch. My migration branch didn’t move. My dev server kept running. Nothing was stashed because nothing needed to be.

Then:

cd ../try-ai-receptionist-hotfix
# fix the bug like a normal person
git add .
git commit -m "fix: null check on booking lookup"
git push origin main
cd -

And I was back in my migration, exactly where I left it. The whole interruption cost me the time it took to actually fix the bug, plus roughly nothing.

Cleanup afterwards:

git worktree remove ../try-ai-receptionist-hotfix

git worktree list shows you everything that's checked out if you lose track.

Things that tripped me up (so they don’t trip you)

The worktree is a fresh directory, and a few things you take for granted aren’t in it.

node_modules. Not there. You have to install dependencies again in the new folder. I’m on pnpm so this was a non-event — pnpm’s global store means the install is mostly hardlinks and finishes in seconds. If you’re on plain npm it’ll sting a bit more.

.env files. Gitignored, so they don’t come along either. I had a confused minute wondering why the app wouldn’t boot before realising. cp .env ../try-ai-receptionist-hotfix/.env and move on. If you're in a monorepo, remember the per-package ones too.

The database. This is the one that can actually hurt you. Both worktrees will happily point at the same database, and if your feature branch has pending migrations, running the app from both directories against one DB is a bad time. I’m on Neon, so I just pointed the hotfix worktree at a separate database branch. Whatever Postgres you’re on, keep the two worktrees on separate DBs if the schemas have diverged.

Ports. Two dev servers, one port, second one loses. Override it in one of the worktrees if you want both running. Which, by the way, is half the point — being able to run main and your feature branch side by side and click around both is something stash can never give you.

Same branch twice — not allowed. Git refuses to check out a branch that’s already checked out in another worktree. Annoyed me for a second, then I realised it’s saving me from two directories fighting over one branch ref. Fair enough.

Where else this is useful

Since this afternoon I’ve been thinking about where else worktrees fit, and honestly the hotfix case might be the least interesting one.

Reviewing a colleague’s PR properly — not just reading the diff, but running the thing — without disturbing your own work. Kicking off a full test suite on one branch while you keep coding on another. And if you’re running AI coding agents that make changes autonomously, giving each one its own worktree stops them trampling each other. That last one is quickly becoming the killer use case, I suspect.

One practical note: keep worktrees next to your repo, not inside it. Nesting them inside means your editor, file watchers and linters start seeing a second copy of everything and get weird.

~/projects/
├── try-ai-receptionist/          ← my migration branch lives here
└── try-ai-receptionist-hotfix/   ← main, temporarily

The bit that surprised me

Worktree shipped in Git 2.5. That was 2015. This feature has been sitting on my machine for a decade and I’ve been stash-juggling the whole time.

If any of this sounds familiar — the interrupted feature work, the stash anxiety, the context rebuild — try it next time instead:

git worktree add ../fix main

It’s a cd instead of a mental reboot. That trade is worth taking every single time.

Git Worktree, or: How I Stopped Losing My Afternoon to Hotfixes was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
